query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The evolution of non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys is driven by the transformation of metastable solid solutions into stable intermetallic compounds, which in turn affects their corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior.
generation.mechanism: Transformation of metastable solid solutions into stable intermetallic compounds
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved corrosion resistance and high-temperature oxidation behavior with increasing Mg content
generation.boundary: Alloys with high Mg content (> 50 at. %)
generation.uncertainty: The exact relationship between Mg content and the formation of stable intermetallic compounds, as well as the resulting effects on corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior

falsification_experiment.design: Controlled variable experiment with systematic variation of Mg content
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the corrosion resistance and high-temperature oxidation behavior do not improve with increasing Mg content, the hypothesis is falsified.

Creep resistant Nb-silicide-based alloys should not suffer from pest oxidation and scale spallation. Could these aims be achieved in alloys with simultaneous additions of RMs, Ge, and Sn? The motivation of the research presented in this paper was to provide answers to this question. In this paper we study how the simultaneous addition of Ta, W, Hf, Ge, and Sn affects the microstructure and oxidation of two Nb-silicide-based alloys without Al and Cr. The structure of the paper is as follows. First, the design and selection of the alloys using the alloy design methodology NICE [] is discussed. The experimental details are followed by the results for the as-cast and heat-treated microstructures and the isothermal oxidation of the alloys at 800 and 1200 °C. The discussion considers first the Si macrosegregation in the alloys, then their solidification and heat-treated microstructures, and this is followed by discussion of their oxidation. Predicted microstructures and properties using NICE [] are compared with the experimental data.

Complex concentrated alloys (CCA) represent a new group of materials, with complex microstructures, comprising of a large number of elements []. CCAs extend the established limits of the high entropy alloys (HEAs) concept by allowing a smaller number of elements in the composition and in various proportions, that can deliver mixed structures containing solid solution and well dispersed intermetallic phases. CCAs generally have higher configurational entropy than conventional alloys and are capable of obtaining complex, disordered compositionally complex solid solution structures. CCAs are distinct from conventional alloys in that they are not based on a single major element and rather include several main elements, which allow a high degree of freedom in alloy compositions and properties. Their properties, such as high temperature resistance, corrosion resistance, workability, and low density, offer a remarkable advantage in the use of CCAs for various extreme conditions applications [,]. In recent years, high-entropy alloys (HEAs) that contain fine grains of intermetallic compounds (IMCs) have gained increasing attention as they have been shown to exhibit both high mechanical strength and strong corrosion resistance. One such class of HEAs is that of CuFeTiZrNi alloys. In this study, we have investigated the effect of increasing Ni content on the microstructure, hardness, and corrosion resistance of the CuFeTiZrNix alloys (where x = 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.8, 1.0 in a molar ratio). The alloys used in this study were prepared in an arc melting furnace and then annealed at 900 °C. First-principles calculations of the bulk modulus were also performed for each alloy. The results revealed that increasing the Ni content had several effects. AbstractIn as-cast (AC) or heat-treated (HT) metallic ultra-high temperature materials often “conventional” and complex-concentrated (CC) or high-entropy (HE) solid solutions (sss) are observed. Refractory metal containing bcc sss also are contaminated with oxygen. This paper studied the stability of CC/HE Nbss and the contamination with oxygen of Nbss in RM(INb)ICs, RM(Nb)ICs/RCCAs and RM(Nb)ICs/RHEAs. “Conventional” and CC/HE Nbss were compared. “Conventional” Nbss can be Ti-rich only in AC alloys. Ti-rich Nbss is not observed in HT alloys. In B containing alloys the Ti-rich Nbss is usually CC/HE. The CC/HE Nbss is stable in HT alloys with simultaneous addition of Mo, W with Hf, Ge+Sn. The implications for alloy design of correlations between the parameter δ of “conventional” and CC/HE Nbss with the B or the Ge+Sn concentration in the Nbss and of relationships of other solutes with the B or Ge+Sn content are discussed. The CC/HE Nbss has low Δχ, VEC and Ω and high ΔSmix, |ΔHmix| and δ parameters, and is formed in alloys that have high entropy of mixing. decision.trend: Research on Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys has focused on their mechanical properties, but there is a growing interest in understanding their corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior. Earlier studies have explored the effects of composition and processing on the microstructure and properties of these alloys. Recent work has highlighted the importance of considering the stability of complex concentrated solid solutions and the contamination with oxygen in refractory metal intermetallic composites. The use of computational models, such as CALPHAD and Monte Carlo simulations, has become increasingly popular for predicting phase evolution and optimizing alloy design. Experimental techniques, including ball milling and spark plasma sintering, have been employed to synthesize and characterize these alloys.
decision.unsolved: Despite the progress made, there is still a lack of understanding of the transformation pathways and the effects of constituent-property differences on the corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior of Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys. The development of a mechanistic hypothesis that can explain the evolution of these alloys and its impact on their properties remains an open question.
decision.lever: investigating the effect of Mg content on the corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior of lightweight high-entropy alloys
decision.why: This next step follows from the trend of researching the corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior of Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys. By systematically varying the Mg content and characterizing the resulting microstructure and properties, researchers can gain a deeper understanding of the underlying mechanisms and develop a mechanistic hypothesis to explain the evolution of these alloys.
